title: Elbow — AP
summary: Three bones, one joint capsule, and the six ossification centres you have to know in order.
text:
A left elbow. Three separate articulations share one capsule: the humero-ulnar joint (trochlea in the trochlear notch – a hinge), the humero-radial joint (capitulum on the radial head), and the proximal radio-ulnar joint, where the radial head spins inside the anular ligament during pronation and supination.

The radius is lateral. On this left limb that puts it on the right of the image; the medial epicondyle – with the ulnar nerve running in a groove behind it – is on the left.

In a child six ossification centres develop around the elbow and they appear in a fixed order: CRITOE.
reading: CRITOE – Capitellum, Radial head, Internal (medial) epicondyle, Trochlea, Olecranon, External (lateral) epicondyle – appearing at roughly 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 years. A trochlear centre with no medial epicondyle means the epicondyle has been avulsed.
The radiocapitellar line: a line up the radial shaft must point at the capitellum in every projection. If it misses, the radial head is dislocated.
On the lateral view the anterior humeral line should cross the middle third of the capitellum; if it passes in front of it, there is a supracondylar fracture.
A visible posterior fat pad is always abnormal: it means an effusion, and in trauma that means a fracture even if you cannot see one.
Then trace every cortex – supracondylar fracture in a child, radial head fracture in an adult.

title: Wrist — lateral
summary: One straight line through four bones, and the angles that reveal a carpal injury.
text:
A left wrist, volar (palmar) to the left, dorsal to the right. The value of this view is alignment: in a normal wrist the axes of the radius, lunate, capitate and third metacarpal lie almost in one straight line, and the scapholunate angle is 30–60°.

The distal radius normally tilts about 11° volar. Lose that – dorsal tilt with dorsal displacement – and you have a Colles fracture; volar tilt and displacement is a Smith.
reading: Radius–lunate–capitate–third metacarpal should be colinear. A lunate tipped dorsally is a DISI pattern (scapholunate injury); tipped volarly, a VISI.
Scapholunate angle 30–60°: over 70° means the scaphoid has flexed away from the lunate.
Volar tilt of the distal radial articular surface about 11°; check displacement and angulation of any fracture in both planes.
A lunate that has rotated into a triangular 'pie' shape on the PA and tipped volarly on the lateral is a perilunate or lunate dislocation – easy to miss, and a surgical emergency.
Look for a volar soft-tissue swelling or a displaced pronator quadratus line as the only sign of an occult fracture.

title: Knee — lateral
summary: The view that finds the effusion, the patellar height and the tibial slope.
text:
A right knee, anterior to the left. The condyles superimpose, so this view is about the soft tissues and the sagittal relationships rather than the bone contours.

Above the patella lies the suprapatellar pouch, continuous with the joint cavity. On a horizontal-beam lateral, fat floating on blood there – a lipohaemarthrosis – means marrow has been opened, so there is an intra-articular fracture even when you cannot see the line.

The dense oblique line across the intercondylar roof is Blumensaat's line; the ACL runs parallel to it.
reading: Look first at the suprapatellar pouch: any soft-tissue density over about 5 mm is an effusion, and a fat–fluid level is a fracture.

Patellar height (Insall–Salvati): the patellar ligament should be no more than 1.2 times the length of the patella. A high patella suggests a ruptured ligament, a low one a ruptured quadriceps tendon.
Blumensaat's line, and whether the patella's lower pole sits at that level in extension.
The tibial plateau slopes about 10° posteriorly – a posteriorly depressed plateau fragment is easy to miss here.
Then the cortices of femur, tibia, fibular head and patella, and finally the fabella and any loose bodies in the posterior joint.

title: Foot — lateral, weight-bearing
summary: A weight-bearing film: the arch is only meaningful when it is loaded.
text:
A right foot, standing on the film. Toes to the left, heel to the right.

The talus transmits the whole body weight and has no muscle attached to it – every muscle passes it by. Like the scaphoid, its blood supply enters distally, so a displaced talar neck fracture starves the body of the talus.

Weight-bearing matters: the medial longitudinal arch is held by bone shape, the plantar ligaments and the plantar fascia, and only a loaded film shows whether it holds. A calcaneal-inclination angle below about 18° is a flat foot.
reading: Check the arch: draw the calcaneal inclination angle from the plantar surface, and Meary's line along the axes of the talus and first metatarsal – normally straight.
Böhler's angle at the calcaneus is normally 20–40°; a calcaneal fracture flattens it.
The lucent triangle of the sinus tarsi should be clear; filling it is a sign of subtalar injury.
Follow the posterior facet of the subtalar joint, the talar dome, the anterior process of the calcaneus and the base of the fifth metatarsal – all common fracture sites that are easy to skate over.
Finally the soft tissues: heel pad thickness, the Achilles insertion and any plantar calcaneal spur.

title: Pelvis — AP
summary: A ring of bone: read it as three rings and five lines, not as a collection of bones.
text:
The pelvis is a ring, and rings fail in two places. So any single fracture you find on this film obliges you to look for the second one – often on the opposite side, often at the sacroiliac joint or a pubic ramus.

Read it as three rings: the pelvic inlet and the two obturator foramina. Each should be a smooth, continuous curve.

The sacroiliac joints transmit body weight from the spine to the legs and barely move; the pubic symphysis is a fibrocartilaginous joint, normally under 5 mm wide in an adult.
reading: The three rings: pelvic inlet, then each obturator foramen. Follow each outline all the way round.
Shenton's line on both sides – the femoral neck curving smoothly onto the inferior border of the superior pubic ramus.
The sacral arcuate lines (the curved cortices of the sacral foramina); a break in them means a sacral fracture.
Symmetry of the sacroiliac joints and a symphysis under 5 mm. Widening of both means an open-book injury.
Then the femoral necks, both acetabula, the iliac crests and the pubic rami; and remember a pelvic fracture usually means significant blood loss.
